build: Cascade Games UK disk, labelled v1.1L by the C64 Preservation Project

exclude: zero page, the stack and pages 2 to 8: the game's variables, never loaded; $30D9 clears zero page and pages 2 to 4 at each start, and no recorded run touches pages 5 to 8
the two screens the game draws into and shows in turn; at the hand-over they hold the end of the loading picture
under the I/O chips, never read: every byte is $FD, a zero byte on the disk after the loader's EOR $FD
never loaded or used: the RAM's power-on pattern

comments.text: The loader jumps here ($7FFE holds $0900). Jumps over the options and high-score records to the start-up code at $098B.

The options record, 17 bytes, $0903-$0913: the word OPTIONS in plain ASCII as a signature, then crash detection ($090A), combatants ($090B), planes each ($090C), the computer's skill ($090D), the scenario ($090E), missile hits to kill ($090F) and four more bytes ($0910-$0913) that are copied and saved with the rest. Start-up ($09CD) takes the record from the disk's copy at $CE00 when the disk's first eight bytes match these; saving ($1E98) writes it to track 18, sector 2. The values here are the ones the program was built with; the disk's copy replaces them.
Option: crash detection, 1 on, 0 off (the options screen toggles it, $29C6).
Option: combatants, 0 one player (the computer flies plane two), 1 two players ($29BD toggles it).
Option: planes each pilot starts with, 3 to 20 ($29CF); copied to the planes-left counters $02F0/$02F1 when a game starts ($0C32).
Option: the computer opponent's skill level, 1 to 20 ($29A8 steps it, only with one player); demo mode sets 20.
Option: the combat scenario, 0 the close-range dogfight, 1 the full-scale aerial and ground attack ($29DF toggles it).
Option: missile hits to kill an aircraft, 1 to 3 ($29E8); $263C indexes the damage table at $7009 with it.
Four bytes at the end of the options record ($0D, $00, $09, $09), copied from the disk and saved with it; no instruction names them.
Bytes after the options record: plain ASCII that reads "INC SAVESTRI", left over from the assembler's buffer. Nothing reads them.

The high-score table, 86 bytes, $0920-$0975: "HIGHSCORES" in plain ASCII as a signature, five scores as 16-bit words in tens ($092A-$0933, highest first), five names of twelve enciphered letters each ended by $FF ($0934-$0974), and the immortal flag $0975. Start-up ($09E5) replaces it with the disk's copy at $CF00 when the signature matches; a new entry saves it to track 18, sector 3 ($1F30). The built-in names all read CASCADE and the scores are 500 down to 100; the disk's copy has the table the title shows.
Five high scores, 16-bit little-endian words counted in tens of points (the screen adds a zero), highest first.
The high bytes of the five high scores, read with $092A (scores are words in tens of points: 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 at the hand-over, 500 to 100 points on screen).
Five names, 13 bytes each: twelve letters in the game's letter cipher (deciphered through $6F7F) and an $FF terminator.

The immortal flag, 0 or 1. The game sets it at $5643 when the name buffer ($6933) begins with the eight letters at $6A30 (DUSTY BU), which $5634 checks after every game whether or not a name was entered, and start-up's copy of the saved high-score table ($09F4-$09FB) loads it from the disk; nothing clears it. While it is set, plane one does not die (checked at $0D93), burns no fuel ($44C6), the side panel says IMMORTAL ($1C5C), and whenever a plane's damage reaches 255 plane one's damage is cleared first ($2809). It sits inside the high-score block, so saving the table writes it to the disk.
Demo mode: 1 while the computer flies both planes between title pages ($0BCA sets it), 0 in a real game ($0BBE).
Eight bytes swapped with $74F1 for demo mode: $0BF6 copies $74F1-$74F8 here when the demo starts and $598A copies them back when it ends.
Eight bytes that hold the real options ($090A-$0911) while the demo runs with its own settings ($0BCF); $598A puts them back.

Which title page is showing: $FF before the first, then 0-4 for the text pages (THE ULTIMATE HEAD TO HEAD CONFLICT; CREATED BY CASCADE GAMES 1987; PROGRAMMED AND DESIGNED BY IAN MARTIN; GRAPHICS BY DAMON REDMOND; TITLE MUSIC BY ROB HUBBARD; three lines each from the pointer tables at $6740, $674A and $6754), 5 for the high-score table, and at 11 the demo starts ($0AF7).
$34, copied to zero page $3D by $30F0; with $439A ($FF) it makes the pointer $FF34, through which $0A2F writes the NMI and reset vectors at $FFFA-$FFFD without naming them.
1 when the title pages restart from the high-score table (after a name was entered, $0A05), 0 to start from the first page ($0A01).
Colour-code tries left, 3 at load; each wrong answer takes one ($3867) and the last wipes memory; a right answer sets it to 0 ($38BB), so the question is asked once per load.

Start-up, run once from the hand-over. Sets the stack, banks out BASIC and the KERNAL ($01 = $35), and stores $FF, or $D4 on an NTSC machine ($02A6 = 0), as the operand at $4435 and $43D6: the interrupt handlers add it plus one to the counter $BF and run the music and the once-a-tick work on each carry, so a PAL machine runs them every frame and an NTSC one on 213 frames in 256: 50 times a second on both, which keeps the tempo and the game's clocks the same. Asks for the title music ($40 in $E574 and $4EAD), starts CIA 1 timer A free-running from $FFFF (the random number source, $5F3B), selects VIC bank 2 ($8000-$BFFF) through CIA 2, then takes the options record and the high-score table from the disk's copies at $CE00 and $CF00 when their signatures match, and goes to $6042.
Options: compare the first eight bytes at $CE00 with the record's ($0903-$090A, which includes the crash-detection byte) and copy all 17 when they match.
High scores: compare the ten signature bytes at $CF00 with "HIGHSCORES" and copy all 86 bytes when they match.

Restart from the first title page; reached after a game ends, from the options screen's SAVE, and after a wrong colour code wipes memory. $0A05 is the entry that starts at the high-score table instead.
Restart the title sequence at the high-score table (after a name has been entered, $565D).

Common title set-up: stack reset, CIA interrupts off, screen and sprites off, zero page and pages 2-4 cleared ($30D9), music state checked ($1F8E), then the NMI vector set to $2AA6 and the reset vector to $603F through the pointer at $3D (= $FF34, plus $C6 and $C8). Waits for both fire buttons to be released, starts the title raster interrupt at $439B on line 252, sets the title screen up and copies 256 bytes from under the I/O ($D000-$D1FF, read with $01 = $34) to $A680 and $B680, then puts the title's sprites ($74B2, $74E1) up.
With all ROM and I/O banked out, copy $D000-$D0FF to $A680 and $D100-$D1FF to $B680: graphics kept in the RAM under the I/O chips until now.

Title page loop: a fire press on either joystick ($030F, edge against $031F) opens the options screen ($0B67); otherwise, each time the page timer zpp_91 reaches 5, the next page comes up: for pages 0-4 the screen effect at $2AC7, three text lines from the tables at $6740/$674A/$6754 (s_35C7) and the effect at $2B29; at page 5 the high-score table ($5738); at page 11 the demo ($0BCA).

The options screen: blank, clear the colours ($1D0D with 15), border black, background dark grey, then loop: draw the screen ($635D), and unless COMMENCE CONFLICT has been chosen ($0224), mark the cursor line ($2A50), act on the stick ($2970), wait for the frame and repeat.

COMMENCE CONFLICT: the colour-code question ($37E1, which returns at once once it has been answered), demo off, the music stopped and the sound effects started unless in the demo ($1F9C), the sound chip cleared ($4E2C), and on to the game set-up at $0BFF.

Start demo mode: set the demo flag, keep the real options in $097F, play a one-player dogfight against the computer at skill 20 with three planes each and one hit to kill, swap in eight bytes from $74F1, and fall into the game set-up.

Set up a game (from COMMENCE CONFLICT or the demo): swap the panel character set in from under the I/O ($53D4), black screen, sprites off, multicolour text mode, zero page and pages 2-4 cleared ($30D9), fire treated as held for both sticks so a press still down does not count, planes left from the options ($090C), the raster chain for the two halves of the screen started at $4902 and $499D, the play interrupt at $43FC on line 252, the left ten columns of colour RAM white, both screens filled with character 10 ($5711), the first 128 bytes of the character set at $B000 copied to $8800 and $A000, sprites set up ($1BF8), both pilots on their hangar screens (state 3), fuel full ($0284/$0285 = $FF), six chaff and six flares each ($0288-$028B), the ground targets placed in the full-scale game ($308C), the hangar cursors on TAKE OFF ($0256/$0257 = 10), and the stick's top turn rate ($022B) 24, or 30 in the full-scale game.

The main loop; a pass takes at least one frame ($24). Plane one's half, then plane two's, then the shared work. For plane one: the plane's 32-byte record at $0300 is copied to zero page $60-$7F, its screen rows are 0-7 ($C4/$C5), $D1 = 0 (this plane) and $55 = 1 (the other). The view state ($46: 0 cockpit, 1 map, 2 shot down, 3 hangar, 4 arming, or ALL AIRCRAFT DESTROYED when the pilot has no planes left) chooses the work: flying states run the checks and controls below; the others run their screens from $0E1D.

Plane one flying (state 0 or 1): the warnings and the damage ($282F), message 31 (a blank) kept in the message rotation, the map square under the plane ($14AF), landing ($1FAD, which ends the flight when the plane is down), a return to the hangar ordered when the other plane was shot down in the full-scale game ($0250), then the controls: the stick ($1DE3, $596C, $594F), Q for flares and chaff ($2531), F and S for power ($4252), E for the weapon ($5F58), the turn and pitch ($28E0, $29FC, $30AC). A crash or a kill ($3A) sends the plane to state 2 and scores the other pilot ($213A), unless the immortal flag is set.
X toggles plane one between the cockpit and the map (states 0 and 1), on the press only (the last state is kept in $64).

Plane one in the cockpit: draw the view into the character set at $A000 or $B000 (whichever is not being shown, $59), through $6225; with Q held show the flare and chaff counts (message 22); put back the four rows of the instrument panel's screen codes from $93D8 when either screen's copy has been overwritten (one cell of each is compared); copy the 93 bytes of instrument graphics at $03A0 into the character set at $A248.
Plane one on the map: rows 0-12 ($C5 = 12), drawn by $13EA.

Plane one not flying: in the demo the computer pilot still runs ($596C). State 2 (shot down) waits for the explosion's time ($02F2 reaching $82), then takes one of the pilot's planes ($2071, $02F0) and returns to the hangar; with none left it shows ALL AIRCRAFT DESTROYED (state 4) or ends the game when the other pilot has none either ($54C0). State 3 is the hangar: in the dogfight PRESS FIRE TO TAKE OFF, in the full-scale game the TAKE OFF and ARM AIRCRAFT menu ($1FFC). With no planes left it shows MISSION COMPLETED - PRESS FIRE, and fire ends the game. State 4 is the arming screen ($5852), or ALL AIRCRAFT DESTROYED ($6339). Then the SAM sites ($64CD) and the mission check ($64B4): when the other pilot has no planes and its ground target is gone, this pilot's hangar shows MISSION COMPLETED (its planes set to 0).

Plane one's hangar screen: clear the view ($20FB), draw the hangar picture's screen codes from $F2B3 ($1BD1, 9 rows), and with planes left draw TAKE OFF and ARM AIRCRAFT ($1FFC) or, in the dogfight, PRESS FIRE TO TAKE OFF; fire takes off ($2F8E puts the plane in the air, $1E11 redraws). With no planes left a fire press ends the game.

End of plane one's part: the ground site's missile launch ($64CD), plane one's missile ($265B), a destroyed ground target's score ($250C), and the check that the other pilot is out of planes and ground targets ($64B4, which ends the mission). Then plane one's zero-page record goes back to $0300.

Plane two's half of the pass, the same work for the record at $0320: screen rows 13-19 ($C4/$C5), $D1 = 1, $55 = 0. Its view state is $47; its keys are H and K for power, U for the weapon, T for flares, V for the map.
Plane two's bearing to plane one, as seen from plane two: $99 turned round by 128 and less plane two's heading gives $98; $9A is negated.
Plane two flying: the instrument and message work as for plane one, and when its weapon selector has reached the chosen weapon ($0F = weapon × 8) the weapon panel is redrawn ($5F89).

Plane two in the cockpit: draw the view into the character set at $A800 or $B800 ($6225), save the turn values ($D9 to $DA, $0E to $9E) and put back its instrument panel's screen codes from $946E the same way.
Plane two not flying: shot down (state 2), the hangar (3) and arming or out of planes (4), as for plane one at $0E1D; the computer pilot takes off by itself after a delay ($1125).

Plane two's hangar screen: the hangar picture's screen codes from $F3C1 ($1BD1, 9 rows), TAKE OFF and ARM AIRCRAFT for a second player, or COMPUTER PILOT - STANDING BY. In the full-scale game the computer arms its plane by chance ($5F3B): a full air-to-air load ($7509) or one with air-to-ground missiles ($750F).
End of plane two's part, as $0F0D: the site's launch, the missile, the target score and the mission check. Then the record goes back to $0320.

Work shared by both planes once a pass: F3 held for ten passes ends the game ($54C0); the engine sounds' pitches ($62A5); the bank indicators ($19A1); F5 held for ten passes switches between the music and the sound effects ($4EAD/$E574); the cockpit messages ($2E57); the instruments ($3C07, $3F2E, $3ED4, $3F62: digits copied to $6D39, $6D63, $6D55); the radar ($3B58, $3A75); the instrument graphics at $03A0-$03FF copied into the character set at $8B2B; and every message timer at $0350 and $0370 counted down.

Wait for the interrupt to finish showing the last frame ($5D), redraw either half whose state changed ($46C8, $4779), then wait for the frame counter $24 to run out (at least two frames a pass) and turn the screen on.

RUN/STOP pauses: the sound is silenced, then the game waits for the key to be released, shows PAUSE ON in the view ($18E0) until RUN/STOP is pressed again, and goes on. In the demo, DEMO MODE is drawn here each pass.

Move a menu cursor with the stick: X and Y give the lowest and highest line, and up or down ($6D) steps the cursor at $0256,X (X = $D1). The stick is compared with $7E, which only the computer's escape sets (to 1, $5EF1) and the zero-page clear zeroes: while they differ, $7B goes back to 1 and the cursor moves on this call; while they are equal, the call waits until $7B has counted to 4. With $7E at 0, as on every menu, a stick held up or down moves the cursor on every call, which off the game ($81 = 0) is held to every fourth frame ($93). With two players the options screen's skill line is stepped over.
After a frame, fill the current plane's half (12 rows of 30 cells from row $C4) with character $23 ($2210).

Part of the cockpit view ($6228): reads two values for the bank angle ($75) from $6FE1 and $6FF1 into $C1/$C2, and adds one to $29 unless the roll is in its second or fourth quarter ($79 odd) with the wings banked ($75 not 0).

Draw the map for the current pilot: the 30 by 12 map picture at $9800 copied into the pilot's half of the screen ($1BD1), the character set at $B000 chosen ($C6), then every object from number $32 down to $33 (counting down and wrapping from 0 to 5; the interrupt turns both, $4469, so a different object is drawn last): each active object's position (across $0296/$029C, down $02A8/$02AE, divided by 8) gives its cell and fine position. Ground target 4 is drawn from the shape at $F7A0 and target 5 from $F7C0, in characters $70 and $74; the planes and missiles (0-3) are drawn only on alternate phases of the blink ($34), through $5FD4, in characters $78 up.

Find what the current plane is over. With the off-map state $0262,X at 2 it does nothing; at 1 it shows FLYING OFF MAP (message 15) and clears the state. Then it reads the map picture under the plane: the row pointer from $71D0/$71DC (Y / 8), the character at X / 8, and the pair of pixels inside that character's shape in the character set at $B000 (row from Y's low byte, pair from X's). Sea (%01) or land (%11) that differs from the last one ($6A) is stored as 0 or 1 in record byte 7 ($0307 or $0327) and in $67, and the view is redrawn ($46B6): the cockpit's ground is blue over the sea and yellow over land ($46D4), and each ground target shows in the view only over its own kind ($61E4: the spy ship over the sea, the radar station over land). Colours %00 and %10 change nothing.
Never called (no instruction or table points here): stores A as the stock of weapon slot X ($0340 + 2X), but 5000 when X is 0 or 4, the two cannons.

Build an object's picture in the work buffer at $0420 (cleared for 32 bytes, or 72 when the size $5E is not 0): the shape's bytes come from a pointer in the table at $7241 (8 bytes per size, 2 per frame; X is the frame, kept in $2C), each looked up through the colour table A/Y, and through the mirror table at $9000 when the frame number is odd (the instruction at $15D0 is NOP then, TYA for even frames).
Low byte of the shape's address, patched by $15AE from the pointer table at $7241.
High byte of the shape's address, patched by $15B4.
Low byte of the colour table the caller gave in A, patched at $1581.
High byte of the colour table the caller gave in Y, patched at $1584.
TYA for an even frame (the shape's byte as it is) or NOP for an odd one (the mirrored byte from $9000 kept), patched by $15C1.
The last byte of each object size's picture ($5E = 0, 1, 2): 7, 31, 71.

Move the picture built at $0420 to its place inside the character cells: down by the top three bits of the low byte of the vertical position ($05, 0-7 rows) and right by 0-3 double-width pixels from the top two bits of the horizontal one ($06). The large size ($5E not 0) swaps the buffer with zero page $B0-$F7 to use zero-page indexing, shifts it there and swaps it back.

Draw an object's picture (A/Y; eight bytes a cell, a column of cells after another) into the current half of the screen: $07 and $08 are the top-left cell, $5E the size (1, 2 or 3 cells a side, $71C1), $5F the first character code to use. Each cell inside rows $C4-$C5 and columns 0-29 gets a fresh character: the background character's eight bytes (from the character set $C6) are copied into it, with the object laid over them where its bytes are not 0, through the multicolour mask table at $9F00, so the background shows round it.
The number of cell rows to draw, patched by $16B2 from $71C1 by the size.
The number of cell columns to draw, patched by $16B5 from the same table.
Low byte of the object's picture, patched by $16A7 from A.
High byte of the object's picture, patched by $16AA from Y.
Low byte of the background character's shape, patched by $1713 when the cell's character changes.
High byte of the background character's shape, patched by $170B.
Low byte of the fresh character's shape (the first character $5F × 8), patched by $16C4.
High byte of the fresh character's shape, patched by $16BF.
Low byte of the background shape for the bytes the object leaves empty, patched by $1716.
High byte of that background shape, patched by $170E.

With the cannon selected ($65 = 0), and for plane two only when its weapon selector has come to rest on the cannon ($0F = 0): set $D9 when the enemy plane is visible ($D8) and within half a cell of the sight's centre (column 15 by $DB and $57, row 4 of the view by $BE and $58), then draw the gun sight's shape ($95C8) at column 14, row 3 ($16A7).

Draw X letters of the string at A/Y into a panel's graphics at ($0C): each letter's five rows come from the small font in page $95 ($6F66 gives each letter's offset), and letters are 32 bytes apart (40 for plane two, $D1 = 1).
Low byte of the message text, patched by $17D1.
High byte of the message text, patched by $17D4.
The letter's offset in the small font's page $95, patched by $17F6 from $6F66.
Low byte of where the letter goes in the panel, from $0C and stepped by the letter spacing ($1804, $180A).
High byte of where the letter goes, from $0D and carried by $1812.
The letter spacing, 32 for plane one or 40 for plane two, patched by $17E1.

The cannon's tracers and hits. Firing ($C0, set at $228D) restarts both counters $0264/$0266 at 3; they count down after the trigger is let go. While either runs, the tracer pictures (one of four frames, $74 and $6EF6) are drawn over the background into four characters at $FF68 and shown in cells round row 4, column 24, and a column of shot marks (characters $CD up) is drawn. The counters are compared with plane one's $0266 for both planes ($18B9). When the enemy is in the sight ($D9), each pass has a one in four chance ($5F3B below $40) of a hit: 20 damage with timer 8 to the other plane ($27FB) and 20 points ($1C25).
The tracer frame's mask offset in $9D48, patched by $185A from $6EF6.
The page of the character set the tracer cells are built in ($C6 + 6), patched by $1879.

Print nine characters of the string at A/Y on row X of the left panel, on both screens ($8000 and $8400): values 0-9 as the digits, letters deciphered through $6F7F, each mapped to a screen code through $73B1.
Low byte of the panel string, patched by $18E0.
High byte of the panel string, patched by $18E3.

Choose the radar scope for the current plane and copy its 94 bytes to $03A0: plane one from $9B28 (or $9E68 when $0487 is set and the distance $94/$95 is $0180 or more), plane two from $ED00 (or $ED60 by $048B the same way); sets the limits $B9-$BC and $BD (1 for the second scope).
Low byte of the chosen instrument template, patched by $1959.
High byte of the chosen instrument template, patched by $195C.

Draw both planes' bank indicators: one of the pictures listed at $654E (plane one) and $6556 (plane two), chosen through $655E by the bank angle (record byte $15), written into the panel graphics ($A1F0, and $8C48 over $9DC8 for plane two) through index tables chosen by the quarter of the roll (byte $19), for plane one in page $97 ($7145) and for plane two at $7389, $7301, $72A1 and $7259 ($656E, $6572), and mirrored through $9000 in quarters 0 and 1. Every fourth pass ($1F) it also redraws the slow instruments ($1A28).
Low byte of plane one's bank picture, patched by $19AC from $654E.
High byte of plane one's bank picture, patched by $19B2.
TYA (not mirrored) or NOP (mirrored) for plane one's bank picture by its roll quarter, patched by $19C0.
Low byte of the index table in page $97 for plane one's bank picture, patched by $19C6 from $7145.
Low byte of plane two's bank picture, patched by $19E6 from $6556.
High byte of plane two's bank picture, patched by $19EC.
TYA or NOP for plane two's bank picture, patched by $19FA.
Low byte of plane two's index table, patched by $1A00 from $656E.
High byte of plane two's index table, patched by $1A06 from $6572.

The slow instruments for both pilots. Plane one: the altitude's five digits ($6D63), the speed's four digits ($42/$44 through $3ED4), the pitch ladder (20 rows at $A2D9 with a mark at the row from $7155 or $716D by the pitch, record byte $17, the table chosen by bytes 3 and $1C), the power bar when the throttle ($0308) has changed, the fuel bar when the fuel ($0284) has changed, and the compass when the heading ($02EA) has changed (heading / 8: one of the pictures listed at $7189 chosen through $71A5, mirrored through $9000 for the second half of the circle).
Low byte of plane one's compass picture, patched by $1AC2 from $7189.
High byte of plane one's compass picture, patched by $1AC8.
TYA or NOP: plane one's compass mirrored for the second half of the circle, patched by $1AE1.
Low byte of the index table in page $97 for the compass, patched by $1AD4 from $71B5.
The same for plane two: altitude ($6D55), speed ($43/$45), power ($0328), fuel ($0285), pitch ladder ($8C22) and compass ($02EB, pictures listed at $7197).
Low byte of plane two's compass picture, patched by $1B93 from $7197.
High byte of plane two's compass picture, patched by $1B99.
TYA or NOP: plane two's compass mirrored, patched by $1BB8.
Low byte of plane two's compass index table, patched by $1BA5 from $71B9.
High byte of plane two's compass index table, patched by $1BAB from $71BD.
Copy X rows of 30 screen codes from the address A + 256 × $AF to the current half of the screen, starting at row Y + $C4, column 10.

Sprites for the game: all off, in front of the background, unexpanded, sprites 6 and 7 multicolour; colours 0 (black) for sprites 0-5 and 9 (brown) for 6 and 7; multicolours 8 (orange) and 7 (yellow).
Add A (in tens of points) to pilot X's score ($025A/$025C), stopping at 65535, and ask for both side panels to be redrawn ($0223 = 2).

Redraw the current pilot's side panel ($0223 counts the redraws still owed). Plane one: PILOT ONE, PLANES and the planes left (IMMORTAL in their place when the flag at $0975 is set), SCORE and the score. Plane two: the planes left, then COMPUTER and LEVEL with the skill when the computer flies it outside the demo, otherwise PILOT TWO, SCORE and the score. A score is shown as its five digits between zeros, ten times the stored number.
Put the current pilot's planes left ($02F0,X) as two digits into the PLANES string ($6BDD) and return its address in A/Y.
Fill colour RAM's 25 rows of 40 with the colour in A.
The colour to fill colour RAM with, patched by $1D0D.
Point $C3 at the screen being drawn: $80 or $84, the one the interrupt is not showing ($59 bit 7).
Set the text printer's column (X), row (Y) and colour (A).
Scan the whole keyboard and return in $2D the number (8 × column + row, counted from 0) of the last key found down, or $40 for none; used by the name entry.

The computer pilot's height keeping: A/Y is the height wanted (800 feet when the high byte is below 3). Unless the plane is banked 7 or more, subtract the plane's altitude ($02DE/$02E4, $581A) and ask $217C to pitch towards it: the difference's high byte, up to 17, or 1 between 100 and 255 feet; within 100 feet it levels the nose when the pitch is below 2.
Wait for the next frame: set $54 and wait for the interrupt to clear it.
From the quarter of the roll ($79, 0-3): $63 = 1 in quarters 1 and 2 and $CD = 1 in quarters 1 and 3.
Set object X's height to A/Y plus a random 0-1023 ($5F3B).
Clear the current pilot's half of the screen that is being shown: swap the screens' roles ($59), fill 12 rows with character 10 ($2210) and swap back.

Never called: stores A/Y as a string pointer, sends "I" (initialise) to drive 8's command channel through the KERNAL's LISTEN, SECOND and CIOUT, then the string at the pointer up to an $FF. Left from another way of using the disk.
Low byte of the unused disk command string, patched by $1E2E.
High byte of the unused disk command string, patched by $1E31.

Hand the machine back to the KERNAL for a disk write: sound stopped ($1F9C, $4E2C), the screen blanked, interrupts off, CIA 1's interrupts off, zero page replaced by the KERNAL's copy at $F900, the KERNAL's vectors at $0300-$033F restored from $65AE, the ROMs banked in ($01 = $37) and the raster interrupt off.

SAVE OPTIONS: the panel character set swapped out ($53D4), the KERNAL brought back ($1E62), the 17 bytes of the options record ($0903-$0913) copied to $CF00, and that buffer written to track 18 sector 2 ($1EC4 with "2"); then the ROMs banked out, the title music asked for again ($E574/$4EAD = $40) and the screen on.

Write the 256 bytes at $CF00 to the disk: open the command channel (15) and a buffer channel (5, name "#"), send the bytes in the order $CF01-$CFFF then $CF00, then send "U2:5,0,18,n" (block write from channel 5 to drive 0, track 18, sector n from $1F2E) and close both.
"U2:5,0,18," and the sector number, which the callers set: "2" for the options, "3" for the high scores.
The sector of the block write: "2" or "3" ($58, "X", in the file).
"#": the name that opens a buffer in the drive.

Save the high-score table: the KERNAL brought back ($1E62), the table at $0920-$0975 (signature, scores, names and the immortal flag) copied to $CF00 and written to track 18 sector 3 ($1EC4 with "3"); then the ROMs banked out, the title music asked for again and the screen on.
Seven bytes no code reads: $60 (an RTS), then "S0:Z", $FF, "Z": a scratch command to the drive for a file called Z, left from an earlier way of saving.
Move an object's position ($06/$07 across, $05/$08 down, in 256ths of a cell) up and left by half its size ($5E: 0 half a cell, 1 one cell, 2 one and a half), so it is drawn centred on its position.
If the music is stopped ($E574 bit 7, the sound effects running), ask for it again: $40 into $E574 and $4EAD.
Outside the demo, stop the music and switch to the sound effects ($C0 into $E574 and $4EAD), and start the engine sound ($4DFB).

Landing: only over a place where the plane can land ($0262,X at 2 or more, set elsewhere). Below 1024 feet ($02E4 under 4) with the pitch below 4 it shows OK FOR LANDING (message 24) and sets $6B; with the wings level ($75 = 0) and upright ($63 = 0) the plane lands: it is reset for the hangar ($208E), its view goes to the hangar (state 3) and A = 1. Higher or steeper it shows REDUCE ALT and TO LAND (messages 7 and 8). A = 0 when the plane did not land.

The full-scale game's hangar menu: lines 10 and 11, TAKE OFF and ARM AIRCRAFT, moved between with the stick ($1363), the cursor drawn by $2A6F. Fire on ARM AIRCRAFT sets $0252 to 1 and the view to the arming screen (state 4); fire on TAKE OFF sets $0252 to 2, which the caller turns into a take-off.
Make A the current weapon ($65) and redraw the weapon panel ($5F89).
A pilot was shot down: outside the demo reset the plane for the hangar ($208E), and clear the other pilot's return-to-hangar flag ($0250), setting it to 1 in the dogfight.

Reset pilot X's plane for the hangar: $021B/$021C = $4268, view state 3, both missiles ($02B6/$02B7) and $91 cleared, the plane's damage, explosion and cannon counters cleared, the plane inactive ($02B4), the hangar cursor on TAKE OFF ($0256 = 10), fuel full ($0284/$0286 = $FF), six chaff and six flares, the other plane's explosion counter cleared, the zero-page record $60-$7F cleared with fire treated as held, and the pilot's message timers ($0350 or $0370) cleared.
Fill three rows (rows 9-11 of the current half, columns 10-39) with character 10.
Start an explosion at the position in $05-$08 for object X: kept in $027C/$027E/$0280/$0282, and its flag $0278 set.
Start object X's explosion counter $027A: 1 for objects 0-5 (A below 6), $20 for others.
Step the current plane's explosion counter $027A: from 1 it counts to $1F, from $20 to $27, then the explosion ends ($0278 and $027A cleared).
Point $C9/$CA at row Y, column 10 of the screen being drawn ($703F/$7058 and $C3).

The computer pilot's elevator: A is the pitch wanted ($36), X its direction (0 or 1). Sets the stick's vertical $6D to -1, 0 or 1 to reach it: first back through zero if the plane is pitched the other way ($7C), then towards the wanted pitch.

The computer pilot's throttle: compare A with the throttle $68 and press this plane's power keys: more (F, $0205; K, $0207 for plane two) when A is higher, less (S, $0204; H, $0206) when lower, neither when equal.
The high byte of character A's shape in the current character set (A × 8 + 256 × $C6); the low byte is left in $AE.
Add 40 to the pointer $C9/$CA: the next screen row.
Subtract 40 from the pointer $C9/$CA: the row above.
Fill X rows of the current half (from row $C4, columns 10-39) with character A.
The fill character, patched by $2210.
Low byte of the row being filled, from $703F and stepped by 40 ($222E, $2234).
High byte of the row being filled, from $7058 plus the screen's page.

The trigger. The weapon panel is refreshed while the trigger is up ($70 = 0); a press arms it ($70). With the trigger held and the current weapon's stock not zero (slot $65, plus 4 for plane two, at $0340), the cannon sets $C0 for this pass ($181B fires it). A missile launches only when none of this plane's is in flight and the target is locked ($17): it starts at the plane's position and 40 feet below it (object 2 or 3), is pushed out sideways to the left or the right wing in turn (the heading plus or minus $30 by the stock's lowest bit, moved once by $3E55 and $3D57), flies on the plane's heading at the plane's speed / 8 ($1A), the other plane's missile warnings are raised ($0483/$048B, or $0487/$048F), one is taken from the stock and MISSILE LAUNCH (message 23) shows. Plane two fires only once its sliding weapon selector has reached the weapon ($0F = weapon × 8).

Draw the missile sight's box round the enemy plane when it is in view ($18) and a missile is selected: the enemy's cell column ($DB) must be 11-18 and its row ($BE, within the half) 2-9; the box (shape from $71E8 by the fine position, characters $D1 up, size 2) is held inside columns 11-16.5 and rows 1-6, and $0E is set to say the enemy is boxed.

Per pass, for the current pilot: the gun sight with the cannon ($1769). With no missile in flight: lock cleared ($17), the range read-out ($2488); in range (distance $9F below 100, and within 8 for the heat seeker, 25 for the radar missile, 4 for air-to-ground) the box is drawn ($234B), and ten passes with the enemy boxed (air-to-ground also below 2304 feet) lock the target: $17 set and TARGET LOCKED (message 20). Out of range: OUT OF RANGE (28). With a missile in flight: the heat seeker needs nothing more; the radar and air-to-ground missiles need the box kept on the target, and when the enemy leaves it for longer than the lock counter ($71) the lock is broken: the missile is lost and LOCK BROKEN (21) shows.

The range messages: for the air-to-ground missile the radar station's range ($248E first, then RADAR STATION and RANGE, messages 26 and 27, from the table at $0490), otherwise the enemy plane's: with the distance ($95, kept in $9F) below 100, ENEMY PLANE, RANGE and ALT (messages 16, 17 and 18).

The range warnings for the current pilot: $95 (the enemy's distance) into $9F, and below 100 messages 16, 17 and 18 (ENEMY PLANE, its RANGE and ALT) for 3 ticks each; reached from $24AC, which with an air-to-ground or air-to-ship missile selected ($65 = 3) also shows messages 26 and 27 (the target and its RANGE) while this pilot's target is within 100.

A missile Y has reached a ground target X (with $EA = 0 and $EB below 100): the missile is removed and the target's hit count ($023E) goes up; the first hit starts a small explosion (kind 10), the second a big one (kind 1) and the count goes to 3, which starts the target's burning ($250C).
A ground target hit twice burns for 29 passes ($0242 counting from 3 to $20), then disappears ($02B8 cleared) and the other pilot scores 2000 points ($1C25 with 200).

Flares and chaff (A is this pilot's decoy key, Q or T). With no enemy missile in flight the key shows the counts (FLARES n CHAFF n, message 22, the digits written into it). With one in flight (other than an air-to-ground missile): FLARE DROPPED or CHAFF DROPPED while a decoy is working, ENEMY MISSILE (14) and its RANGE (13) when it is close; the key drops chaff against a radar missile (timer 8) and flares against a heat seeker (timer 5), or says NO CHAFF or NO FLARES. Then the hit test: within 100 across ($0482/$0483 by this pilot's index $D4) and 50 feet in height, the missile is removed and does 25-32 to the damage timer and a damage of $7009 by the hits option (255, 128 or 96) through $27FB, starts an explosion, and scores 50 points for the other pilot.

Bug: with no chaff left, the call to $34F8 that shows NO CHAFF returns with X still 11, the message number, and there is no jump past this code, so instead of this pilot's count and timer it decrements $0293 (the low byte of plane two's missile's position across) and writes 8 into $0297 (the middle byte of plane two's position across), whichever pilot pressed the key: plane two moves by less than an eighth of a square of the map.

Fly the current pilot's missile (object 2 + X) when it is active. Air-to-ground missiles go to $27D4. The speed ($0270) rises by 4 a pass to the type's top speed ($7860: 250 for the heat seeker, 255 for the radar missile), and is quartered near the target ($0482/$0483 below 25). A heat seeker lives 14 ticks of $026C and a radar missile 40, then disappears ($2760). A decoy can turn it away: a radar missile meets chaff with a chance of 180 in 256, or 200 for the human pilot's missile against the computer; a heat seeker meets flares within 2 with a chance of 220 in 256, or 230 plus the skill level for the human's missile against the computer. A decoyed missile turns $30 off its course and halves its speed. A locked missile ($17) steers towards the target by up to 5 a pass ($4E); then it moves ($2766, $3E55).
Move the missile's height towards the target's ($50/$52): the speed adds into $025E, and on each carry it climbs $82 or dives $8B feet, or matches the height when it is within $8C.
The air-to-ground missile: speed up by 8 a pass to at most $C0, a life of 20 ticks, then the shared guidance at $271E.

Damage pilot X: A goes to its timer $0254, Y is added to the damage $0276. Reaching 255 kills the plane ($0276 = $FF) and makes the explosion sound ($4DFB, with the demo flag cleared for the call so it sounds in the demo too). With the immortal flag set, plane one's damage is cleared first, which matters when the plane killed is plane two: shooting down the computer repairs the immortal plane.

Per pass: the plane's weight $69 from the three missile stocks ($0342-$0346, the air-to-ground stock through $5949) and plane one's fuel ($0284 / 64, for both planes), CRASH WARNING (message 1) below 2816 feet in a dive steeper than 1, the kill when the damage reached $FF (the other pilot scores 200 points; below 4864 feet a chance of 160 in 256 of a spin, $6B = 2, otherwise the plane is lost at once, $3A), FUEL IS LOW (4) flashing below fuel $30, ENEMY CLOSE (9) when the planes are within $50 across and 100 in height, and a collision ($3A) within $1A and $1E.

The stick's left and right: rolls the plane. Holding it accelerates the roll ($7B, from 4 up to the top rate $022B) and the rate is scaled by the bank ($9C08 or $9C18 by $75, $4349); the bank $75/$76 runs 0-15, and passing either end moves the roll to the next quarter ($79).

The options screen's fire: on the press only, act on the line under the cursor ($0256): 0 COMMENCE CONFLICT ($0224), 1 players, 2 skill (1-20, one player only), 3 scenario, 4 planes (3-20), 5 crash detection, 6 missile hits (1-3), 7 SAVE OPTIONS ($1E98, then back to the title).

The stick's up and down: changes the pitch ($77, 0-18, with its direction $7C). How often it acts depends on the bank ($6F56 adds into $72), and the plane's attitude ($63) decides which way the stick moves the nose. Pulling past 18 takes the plane over the top: the roll moves a quarter ($79) and the heading turns half a circle ($02EA EOR $80).
Draw the options cursor (characters $1E and $1F) at columns 1-2 of the row for the line under the cursor ($65A6).
Draw a menu cursor (characters $1E and $1F) at columns 11-12 of row Y of the current half.
Draw the cursor (characters $1E and $1F) at columns 6-7 of screen row Y.

The NMI handler, which CIA 2's timer A fires a few cycles after $6066 starts it: acknowledges CIA 2, then puts back the two bytes $6066 broke: $85 (STA) at $43FC, the first instruction of the play interrupt, and $EA (NOP) at $16E9 in the object drawer. If the NMI never comes (its vector changed, a freezer cartridge), the play interrupt starts with STX $02 and so returns the wrong A to the main program, and the object drawer returns at once: nothing is drawn.
One byte where the NMI handler keeps A ($2AA6) and from which it takes it back before RTI ($2AC0); the two bytes after it are not used.

A title wipe: two edges of light grey, grey and dark grey (colours 15, 12, 11) close in from both sides of the screen to the middle, one column a frame, leaving black text colour behind them ($3922 colours one column of rows $B5 up to $B7).
A title wipe the other way: the grey edges open from the middle outwards, one column a frame, leaving white text colour behind.
The computer pilot: keep the plane at the height it has ($1D7B with its own altitude).

The computer pilot's turn towards a bearing A (relative to its heading; $2E keeps it). A bank of 15 pulls the stick back; a bank of 9 or more lets the pitch fall a step. Within two steps of the bearing the heading is corrected directly and the wanted bank is 0; within $20 the wanted bank is twice the bearing's size, at most 11; further off it is 15. Then $2C3A banks towards it.

The computer pilot chasing the enemy: when the enemy is behind it ($98 + $40 negative), upright, banked below 8, and with a chance of 32 in 256, plane two at skill 5 or more starts its escape manoeuvre ($B8 = 1, $12 = 0) outside the demo. Otherwise it pursues ($4362) and opens the throttle to $60 when the bearing is more than $18 off.
The computer pilot's throttle in a chase: with the planes close ($95 = 0), plane one's throttle less its byte 9 plus plane two's byte 9; otherwise full ($FF), through $21B6.

The computer pilot's roll towards the bank $2F. Inverted ($63) it pushes the stick right; when the roll is in the quarter that suits the turn (quarter 0 for a positive bearing, 3 for a negative one) it moves the bank $75 itself, up to two steps a pass towards $2F, without touching the stick; otherwise it pushes the stick ($6E) to roll round to that quarter.

Draw the enemy plane in the cockpit view. Only when it is ahead (bearing $98 within $20 either side) and nearer than 25 ($95): its place on the screen from $3948 ($DB/$57 across, $BE/$58 down); an explosion is started there when it has been shot down or is being hit ($0254, $2120). By distance: 6 or more an empty cell; 2 to 5 one or two dots ($5FD4); closer, a medium picture (2 cells, $352C and the shapes at $6576), and nearest (within $78 across and $13 in height) the large picture (3 cells), chosen from the enemy's heading relative to ours ($56), its roll ($0272) and its pitch ($0274) through the view tables at $7816, $7678, $7648, $7608 and $75B0, and built by $1581 and $15DB. $D8 says the medium or large picture is showing and $18 that something was drawn. Then the radar ($3CA1).

The cockpit messages. Counts each pilot's live messages (timers at $0350 and $0370, into $02F4/$02F5). About every 14 passes ($80 adds $12 a pass) each pilot's panel moves on to its next live message, wrapping within 16 when any are live, and draws its two lines of seven letters ($17D1; the text pointers at $7432 and $7472) into the message panel ($A325 for plane one, $8AA0 for plane two), or clears the panel when none is live.

Prepare the current plane for take-off: its weapon stocks loaded from its loadout (dogfight $74E9 or $74F9: 3000 cannon rounds and 8 heat seekers; full-scale $74F1 or $7501: 3000 rounds, 6 heat seekers and 4 radar missiles, which the arming screen changes), fractions and the death timer cleared, the throttle $BF and the speed 500 ($42/$44). In the dogfight it starts at 20,000 feet plus up to 1023 on a random heading, near the middle of the map or within 20 of the other plane when that is flying. In the full-scale game it starts at 1000 feet plus up to 1023 by its base: plane one at across $0A, down $20, heading $40; plane two at across $E8, heading $C0.
Low byte of plane one's loadout for the scenario, patched by $2F9A from $7568.
High byte of plane one's loadout, patched by $2FA0.
Low byte of plane two's loadout, patched by $2FB9 from $756C.
High byte of plane two's loadout, patched by $2FBF.
In the full-scale game, put the two ground targets on the map: target 4 at across $58, down $38, target 5 at across $98, down $10, both active ($02B8/$02B9).

Keep the current plane's attitude for both cockpit views: $0272,X = the roll as 0-63 (the quarter × 16 plus the bank, mirrored in quarters 1 and 3) and $0274,X = the pitch's height change ($6582 by the pitch, negative when diving). The other plane's view reads them with Y to draw this plane ($2D22, $2D30, $353C, $354A); this plane's own view reads them with X = $D1 to choose the enemy's and the ground targets' pictures by its own roll and pitch ($2D74, $2DA6, $356D, $357F, $6135, $617C).
Clear zero page $02-$FB and pages 2 to 4 ($0200-$04FF), then set $3D/$3E from $0988 and $439A.
Colour plane one's view (rows 0-7, columns 10-39 of colour RAM) with A.
Colour plane one's instrument rows (8-11, columns 10-39) with A.

Colour plane two's view with A: colour RAM rows 13-20, columns 10-39. Plane two's view is rows 13-19 ($0F52-$0F58); row 20 is the top row of plane two's panel, which $3149 (rows 21-24) leaves to this routine.
Colour plane two's instrument rows (21-24, columns 10-39) with A.

Draw the horizon across the current pilot's view, as characters. The line's slope comes from the bank ($75, through $6FE1 and $6FF1 scaled by the pitch, $4334) and its place from the pitch: $28 is the column where it crosses and $29 its row. Characters $DC (sky) and $DD (ground) fill each side, swapped in quarters 1 and 3 ($CD); along the line go edge characters, taken for the bank from the lists at $7071 ($708F long), stepping $70E1 columns every $70F1 rows. With the wings level ($75 = 0) the rows are filled with sky above and ground below ($33D9); at bank 15 the line is upright. Last, the edge and fill characters' shapes are copied into the character set ($7111 and $7101, mirrored through $9000 and with the colours swapped by EOR $AA when the plane is inverted), and $D3 is set to say the horizon is in view.
ADC or SBC (opcode $65 or $E5) for the horizon's crossing column, by the slope's sign $F3; patched by $3185.
The view's first row ($C4) plus 3: the row where the horizon line is placed, patched by $3193.
ADC or SBC for the horizon's row, by the sign $F4; patched by $31AD.
Low byte of the edge characters for this bank (left to right), patched by $3212 from $7071.
High byte of the edge characters, patched by $321B.
Low byte of the edge characters read the other way (quarters 1 and 3), patched by $3215.
High byte of the same, patched by $321E.
Low byte of the edge characters' shapes for this bank, patched by $3391 from $7111.
High byte of those shapes, patched by $3397.
TYA or NOP: the edge shapes mirrored when the sky is on the right ($CD), patched by $33A7.
0 or $AA: the edge shapes' colours swapped when the plane is inverted, patched by $3386.
The character set's page plus 6, where the edge shapes go ($F0 up), patched by $33AF.
0 or $AA for the sky and ground shapes, patched by $3383 and $342D.
The page for the sky and ground shapes ($E0 up), patched by $33B2 and $341E.
When the horizon is off the view: fill it with sky or ground (character $E0 plus the pitch direction $7C) and copy the fill shapes from $7101 into the character set; $D3 cleared.
The page for the fill shapes when the horizon is off the view, patched by $3446.

Draw a bar on plane one's instrument panel: A is the value (0-255), X the low byte of its place in page $A1. Four cells, 32 bytes apart, four rows each: full for each 64 of the value, then a partial cell from $7141, then empty; the first cell's left edge is kept.
Low byte of the bar's next cell in page $A1, from X and stepped by 32 ($348E, $3494).
The same bar for plane two's panel in page $8A: cells 40 bytes apart, five rows each, the last cell's right edge kept.
Low byte of plane two's bar's next cell, from X and stepped by 40 ($34E1, $34E7).
High byte of plane two's bar's next cell, from $8A and carried ($34EA, $34EF).

Show message X (0-31, the texts listed at $7432) to the current pilot for Y ticks: the timer goes to $0350,X (plane one) or $0370,X (plane two). When the message was not already live, the pilot's panel is told to show it next ($82 or $83 = X - 1, and $80 = $FF so the change happens on the next pass). Every caller loads X with a fixed number, and none passes 12 (YOU TRAITOR) or 19 (the first TARGET LOCKED); nothing else writes those timers, so those two messages never appear.

Choose the medium-sized picture of the enemy: from its heading relative to ours, its roll ($0272) and its pitch ($0274), and our own roll and pitch, through the tables at $6607, $6637, $6667, $6677, $66A7 and $66D7 to a code from $9358; X returns the picture's pointer number (code / 8) and $A0 the code.

Print the string at A/Y centred on screen row X in the title's two-row letters: each character's top-row codes come from $66BB and its width in cells from $66E5, the bottom row's codes are one more; spaces and punctuation are blank cells ($FF). Both rows are built at $0420 and $0448, the row cleared, then drawn from column (39 - width) / 2 ($3637).
Low byte of the big text's string, patched by $35C7.
High byte of the big text's string, patched by $35CA.
Draw the two rows of big letters built at $0420/$0448 ($A2 cells wide) at column $A0 of the row at $C9/$CA and the row below, clearing both rows first.

Read both joysticks and the keyboard. The last stick values are kept (record bytes $1D-$1F), then the eight keyboard rows are scanned (rows in the order 7, 1-6, 0, kept at $A0-$A7). Joystick port 1 shares $DC01 with the keys, so the OR of all eight scans holds only the stick: a key pulls one row low, the stick all of them. From it and from $DC00 (port 2) come vertical ($030D/$032D: -1 up, +1 down), horizontal ($030E/$032E) and fire ($030F/$032F). Outside a game, in a one-player game, or when neither pilot has planes, port 2 also drives plane one. Then the key flags at $0200-$020D: RUN/STOP, X, V, C=, S, F, H, K, F3, Q, T, E, U, F5. On frames with $59 bit 7 set any stick movement clears F3, F5, RUN/STOP and C=; U clears T and E clears Q.

The colour code security system: three tries ($098A). A square is picked at random from the 40 in the table at $FA00 (four bytes each: column, row, colour); its column and row names are written into the question ($675E and $679E into $68AB-$68AF) and its colour kept in $E0. The cursor ($0256, from $10) moves down the 14 colours with the stick ($1363) and the border shows the colour under it. Fire answers: light green counts as green (13 as 5) and cyan as blue (3 as 6). Right: the tries are cleared and this routine's own code from $37E7 to $38B8 is overwritten with random bytes. Wrong: another square; after the third wrong answer memory from $CFFF down to $0100 is filled with one random byte and the game jumps to $0A01, into the wreckage.
Draw the title logo, 13 by 5 characters from $7515, at row 2, column 13 of the screen at $8000, coloured red.
Colour column X of colour RAM with A in rows $B5 up to $B7, when X is between $A3 and $A4; used by the title wipes.
Low byte of the colour RAM row, patched by $3931 from $700D.
High byte of the colour RAM row ($D8 plus $7026), patched by $393A.

Put a point on the cockpit view: A is its bearing from the plane's nose, Y its elevation (both signed). Scaled through $9BE8 and $6F16 and turned by the plane's roll (the horizon's slopes $C1/$C2 and the roll's quarter, tables $71C4-$71CC), the point is placed relative to where the horizon crosses the view ($28, $29). Returns its cell and fine position in $07/$06 (column) and $08/$05 (row), or a place off the view when it falls outside the current half.

Bearings, elevations and ranges between the planes and the ground targets, four bytes each ($3F97: bearing, elevation, range low, high): plane one to target 4 at $0490, plane two to target 5 at $049C, plane one to target 5 at $0494, plane two to target 4 at $0498. A range below 100 is also written as digits into the RANGE messages ($6DEF, $6DFD). An air-to-ground missile in flight is aimed at its target and tested for a hit ($24DB).

The same for the missiles: plane one to its own missile (object 2) at $0480, plane two to its own (3) at $048C, plane one to plane two's missile at $0484, plane two to plane one's at $0488; the enemy missile's range as digits into the RANGE message ($6D01, $6D0F). Each missile's course to its target ($4E/$4F: the bearing from the missile, against its heading) and the target's height ($50-$53) are kept for its guidance.
The same from plane one to plane two, kept in zero page: bearing from plane one's nose $98, elevation $9A, compass bearing $99, range $94/$95, height difference $96/$97 and its sign $D7.

Draw both missiles for the current pilot ($38 = 1, then 0; the range table entry from $0480 by $D4): a missile within range 8 and within $20 of the nose is drawn in the cockpit view (a shape from $6596 by its range, characters $DA/$DB), and every missile goes on the radar ($3CA1).

Plot a dot on the current pilot's radar scope, on alternate blink phases ($34): X is the bearing, A/Y the range (nothing at 100 or more, ranges of 9 or more drawn at the edge). The range is scaled (×8 unless the close-range template is in use, $BD) and kept at least 4, turned by the bearing through the sine and cosine tables ($92D0, $9310, $4334), offset from the scope's centre ($BB/$BC) and kept inside its limits ($B9/$BA), then set into the panel's graphics (row pointers $65FB, pixel masks $6603). The enemy plane ($0E set) is two pixels tall.

Move object X by its velocity: across by $02BA/$02C0 in the direction $02C6, down by $02CC/$02D2 in the direction $02D8, in 24-bit positions. The map runs from 4 to $EB across and from 4 to $5B down (high bytes). A missile that leaves it is removed. A plane is held at the edge and its off-map state $0262 set: reaching its own side's edge (the left for plane one, the right for plane two) gives 2, where it may land; the far edge, the top or the bottom gives 1, FLYING OFF MAP.

Set object X's velocity from its heading ($02EA: 0 up the map, $40 right, $80 down, $C0 left) and the speed in $39: the direction signs $02C6 (across) and $02D8 (down), and the speed times the heading's sine and cosine ($9BC8, $9BD8, by heading / 8), over 16, into $02BA/$02C0 and $02CC/$02D2.
Turn A/Y (0-65535) into five decimal digits, 0-9 each, at $A9-$AD, by subtracting the powers of ten at $7428/$742D.
Turn a range A/Y into text at $A9: the high byte as digits, a point, and the low byte / 26 as tenths; nothing when the high byte is 100 or more.
Remove the leading zeros (up to four) from the five digits at $A9-$AD and pad the end with spaces.
Never called: blanks the leading zeros of the digits at $A9 in place.

Subtract Y from the current plane's speed, stopping at 0.

The power keys and the plane's motion for a pass. X and Y are this pilot's more and less keys (F and S, or K and H): holding one moves the throttle $68 (0-255) by a step that grows from 4 to 16 while it is held ($61). Then: the speed over 8 ($1A; for plane two the low byte is read from plane one's $42, $42A4) times the pitch's cosine ($6EFE) gives the ground speed $39, which sets the velocity ($3E55). Thrust is the throttle less the bank, halved below the afterburner ($C0) and halved again, times 126 plus the altitude / 512, over 256; drag is the weight $69 times the speed over 8, over 256; half the difference is added to or taken from the speed ($41FB, $4232). The climb rate $4A (at least 1 with the nose off level) is the speed times $740C by the pitch, with its direction in $48. With the nose up the plane loses speed and with it down gains it, a step of the pitch about every third pass ($62 adds $60).

The turn for a plane: X is its bank, A its roll quarter, Y its stick's vertical. The rate is $6ED6 by the bank, plus $6EE6 when the stick is pulled back, minus it when pushed, and negative in quarters 2 and 3; returned as a signed 16-bit A/Y (A low) to add to the heading.

Each 50th call: the chaff and flare timers ($028C, $028E) count down, the seconds counter $0218 counts up to 255, and $91 counts to 60 for the minutes at $0210. In play it is called on each tick of the music clock ($44E9, 50 ticks a second), so the work comes once a second; on the title it is called at every interrupt ($43E7), so the work comes every 50 frames, a second on a PAL machine and about 0.83 of one on NTSC.

Text no code reads, plain ASCII: "WELCOME TO MY CODE. WHAT ARE YOU DOING IN IT? ANYWAY, SINCE YOU ARE HERE, I'LL JUST TELL YOU THAT THIS GAME IS DEDICATED TO THE VERY WONDERFUL TERESA. I SHOULD ALSO LIKE TO THANK EVERYBODY HERE FOR THEIR HELP, AND I'LL SAY THANKS TO OCEAN FOR NOT RELEASING TOPGUN FOR THE C64, AND THANKS TO THE PROGRAMMERS FOR DOING SUCH A BAD JOB. IF YOU'RE READING THIS GUYS, PLAY ACE2, AND SEE HOW THESE SORT OF GAMES SHOULD BE DONE! IF YOU ENTER THE NAME OF MY HAMSTER ON THE HIGH SCORE TABLE, PLAYER ONE WILL BE IMMORTAL. A REAL HACKER WILL FIND HER NAME FROM THE CODE" (the spaces between lines are missing in the bytes).

After both pilots, a new entry saves the table to the disk ($1F30) and shows it; otherwise back to the title.

The full-scale game's AIRCRAFT WEAPONS SELECTION screen (the picture at $F4CF): heat-seeking air-to-air, radar air-to-air, and AIR-GROUND for plane one or AIR-SHIP for plane two, then PREPARE FOR TAKE OFF. Fire on a line adds one of that missile, wrapping at 9, 7 and 3; the load must stay within 16 (one per heat seeker, two per radar missile, 0, 6 or 12 for none, one or two of the third kind, $5949), and carrying the third kind leaves no room for radar missiles. The counts are kept in the loadout ($74F3/$74F5/$74F7, or $7503-$7507) that take-off loads. PREPARE FOR TAKE OFF returns to the hangar.
GROUND in the arming screen's screen codes (the font in the character set at $B800), copied over the picture at $F5C9 for plane one, so its third line reads AIR-GROUND ($5858).

The most of each kind the arming screen allows before it wraps to 0: 9 heat seekers, 7 radar missiles, 3 of the third kind (the fourth byte is the next instruction's).
With no fuel left ($0284,X = 0), hold the less-power key and release the more-power key: the throttle runs down.

Run every pass for each plane. In the demo, fire on either stick ends the demo (the loadout and options put back, $5988); plane one is flown by script from the clock $0218: in the hangar it goes to the arming screen at 5 seconds and takes off after 15, on the arming screen it chooses after 9, and in the air it shows the map at 18 seconds and goes back at 25. Then $5A1C for both planes.

For every plane: in a one-player game plane two's stick and keys are cleared, the computer flies it. On the ground (height 0) with the nose off level it crashes ($3A) when spinning or with crash detection on; with crash detection off it shows PLANE CRASHED and recovers ($6B = 1). While being hit the stick shakes left and right. Below a speed of 140 STALL WARNING and the nose is pushed down. Above 58,880 feet CEILING 60000 and the nose is pushed down now and then. $6B = 1 levels the wings and the nose by itself (after a crash with detection off, or on a landing approach) until level; $6B = 2 is a spin after a kill: CONTROL LOST, nose down, rolling, no firing. Then the computer pilot ($5B47).

The computer's decisions, every other pass ($19), for plane two in a one-player game or both planes in the demo. Low and diving: level the wings and climb to 3000 feet. Off the map: turn round. Otherwise, three times in four, it draws a number from 0 to 21 and acts only when it is below the skill level; when it does not act the stick is centred. Acting, it first meets an enemy missile in flight: against a radar missile always, a heat seeker within range 8, it drops decoys (T, $020A) when the missile is close, or turns its wings level and dives or climbs 78 × 256 feet away from the missile's height with the throttle set from the skill.
In the demo, plane one flies east (heading $40) at 5000 feet with throttle $C0.

Plane two's plan: with fuel below $2E, home at 800 feet ($5E3F). With air-to-ship missiles and the enemy 10 or more away: down to 800 feet, then at the target (bearing $0498), the air-to-ship missile selected and fired. With plane one not flying: towards plane one's side at 30,000 feet, or circling. Plane one 10 or more away: chase with the radar missile and fire when locked ($9E), or chase for the heat seeker, or go home with nothing left; with its own missile in flight it follows, matching height within 200 feet. Closer than 10: the dogfight moves at $5D30.

Close combat. A move is drawn at random ($0227 = 1-4, $0260 a random side): 1 turn hard away; 2 throttle back so the enemy overshoots, climbing when it is close; 3 full throttle and a roll and pull through a loop; 4 a hard turn at 3000 feet. The move is kept while the enemy sits behind it, within 6 × 256 feet in height, range 2 and $30 in heading; otherwise it attacks ($5E2D).

Attack: with no weapons left, home ($5E3F). The escape manoeuvre when $B8 is set ($5EED). With heat seekers and no missile in flight: selected and fired when locked ($9E). Otherwise the cannon: far apart in height, climb or dive to the enemy's height; enemy ahead and heading towards it, turn just past its bearing with the throttle by the range; roughly the same heading, follow it ($2C23) and fire when lined up ($DA); otherwise chase ($2BE1).
Go home: 800 feet, the heading $40 (towards plane two's side), full throttle.
The escape manoeuvre ($B8, chosen at $2BE1 when the enemy is behind): roll past bank 4 until inverted, pull through at full throttle until upright and level, then roll level; then $B8 is cleared.
A second RTS, after the one at $5F39, that no path reaches.
