Masks for a two-pixel-wide dot: $F0 for the left half of a byte, $0F for the right, two of each, for $5FD4.
The screen row of each of the eight lines of the options screen, for the cursor ($2A50): 2, 5, 7, 9, 15, 17, 19 and 22.

A copy of the KERNAL's vectors and work bytes at $0300-$033F as they are after a reset, 64 bytes, put back by $1E62 before the game hands the machine to the KERNAL to write to the disk ($0300 IERROR $E38B, $0314 IRQ $EA31, $0318 NMI $FE47, $031A OPEN $F34A and the rest of the I/O vectors to $0332 SAVE $F5ED). Its last 25 bytes, from $65E2, are also the name cipher, read through $65A1 + the letter: A to Y become S R P Q K C O A W G E D U H M V Y B T F I X N L J.

The radar picture's rows: four pointers, low byte then high byte, into the instrument template copied to $03A0 ($03A0, $03B8, $03D0 and $03E8, 24 bytes apart), picked by $3D2D by the dot's place across.
The high bytes of the radar row pointers, read with $65FB.
The radar dot's pixel mask for each of the four double-pixel places in a byte: $C0, $30, $0C, $03.

The enemy's medium-range picture, first step ($352C): 48 entries, by the enemy's direction relative to ours in quarters (bits 0-1 of the index), its roll quarter (bits 2-3) and its pitch (bits 4-5: 0 near level, 1 climbing, 2 diving), each a row (0, 4, 8 or 12) of the table at $6667.
For the same 48 entries: a quarter (0-3) to which our own roll quarter is added, modulo 4, for the column of the table at $6667.
Sixteen entries, four rows of four: an index (0-36) into the tables at $6677 and $66A7.
For each of those 37 indexes, a row (0, 4, 8, 12 or 16) of the table at $66D7 ($35A9). The 11 bytes from $669C are not read.
For the same 37 indexes, a column (0-2) to which our own pitch adds 0 near level, 1 climbing or 3 diving, modulo 4 ($35AE). The 11 bytes from $66CC are not read.

Read as $66BB + the character ($360D), so its first entry, for 0, is at $66EB: the title font's top-left character code for each character from 0 to Y, 42 bytes (A $00, B $04 and so on four apart, I and J two apart, 1 to 9 from $66, 0 at $8A; the punctuation codes : to @ read 0). Z's entry would be the first byte of the width table below. The bytes from $66BB to $66EA belong to the tables at $66A7 and $66D7.

Twenty entries, $66D7-$66EA, five rows of four: the place in the picture-code table at $9358 for the row and column, whose code / 8 picks the pointer at $6576 and whose low four bits pick the frame ($35B9).

Read as $66E5 + the character ($3612), from $6715 for 0 to $673F for Z: each title-font character's width in cells, 2 for most, 1 for I and J, 3 for W, 0 for @. Each cell is two codes, the top one and the one below it, and the next cell's top code is two more.
The first lines of the five title pages, as pointers low byte then high byte: THE ULTIMATE, CREATED BY, PROGRAMMED AND, GRAPHICS, TITLE MUSIC.
The high bytes of the first-line pointers, read with $6740.
The second lines of the title pages: HEAD TO HEAD, CASCADE GAMES, DESIGNED BY, BY, BY.
The high bytes of the second-line pointers.
The third lines: CONFLICT, 1987, IAN MARTIN, DAMON REDMOND, ROB HUBBARD.
The high bytes of the third-line pointers.

The security grid's column names, two stored characters each, 32 of them: A to Y, then where Z would be the code $5A, which the cipher at $6F7F turns into a 0 byte, then AA, BB, CC, DD, EE and FF. $380D takes the square's column from $FA00, doubles it and copies the name into the question at $68AB. The letters are enciphered and read back through $6F7F, like the game's other screen text.
The second character of each column name, read with $675E: a space for the 26 single-letter names, the letter again for AA to FF.
The grid's row names, two characters each: 1 to 9 with a space after, then 10 to 20; copied into the question at $68AE.
The second character of each row name, read with $679E.

The security question's colour names, each ending in $FF, colours 0 to 13 in the machine's order: BLACK, WHITE, RED, CYAN, PURPLE, DARK GREEN, BLUE, YELLOW, ORANGE, BROWN, PINK, DARK GREY, MEDIUM GREY, LIGHT GREEN (pointers at $54A4). The cursor shows the name under it.

The security screen: " COLOUR CODE SECURITY SYSTEM ", then "ON THE REVERSE  OF THE INLAY CARD IS A", "COLOUR GRID. PRESS FIRE TO INDICATE" and "THE COLOUR AT SQUARE AA 12", whose AA 12 is replaced by the square asked for.
The question's column name, first character, written by $3810.
The column name's second character, written by $3816, and the space after it.
The question's row name, first character, written by $3821.
The row name's second character, written by $3827, and the $FF that ends the line.
The warning under the question: "WARNING! THREE WRONG ANSWERS WILL WIPE  THE GAME FROM THE COMPUTER'S MEMORY...".
The name entry after a top-five score ($54C0): "YOUR SCORE IS ONE OF THE TOP FIVE" and "ENTER YOUR NAME  ", followed by the name field.

The name being entered, ten characters ending in $FF: ten dots until the letters typed replace them, each stored enciphered ($55F9). $5634 compares the first eight with $6A30, and the high-score table keeps the name.

The two scenario descriptions under COMBAT SCENARIO on the options screen, each three lines of forty and an $FF (pointers at $6EBE): "CLOSE RANGE DOGFIGHT. BOTH PLANES ARE ALREADY FLYING, AND ARMED WITH SHORT RANGE MISSILES ONLY." and, from $69B7, "FULL SCALE AERIAL AND AIR-GROUND COMBAT SIMULATION. BOTH AIRCRAFT MUST INTERCEPT, AND ATTACK.".
DUSTY BUG, enciphered, with no end mark: COMMENCE CONFLICT follows at once. $5634 compares only the first eight letters with the name entered, so DUSTY BU is enough to make pilot one immortal.
The options screen's lines, each ending in $FF: COMMENCE CONFLICT, "COMBATANTS: ", ONE PLAYER, TWO PLAYERS and "COMPUTER OPPONENT SKILL LEVEL: " followed by the two digits of the level.
The skill level's first digit, written by $63D4 and $643A.
The skill level's second digit, written by $63D9 and $643F, then the $FF that ends the line.
More options lines: "COMBAT SCENARIO...", "NUMBER OF PLANES EACH: ", "CRASH DETECTION: ", ON, OFF and "MISSILE HITS TO KILL AIRCRAFT: " followed by the number.
The missile hits to kill, one digit, written by $6490; then SAVE THESE OPTIONS TO DISK.

The title pages' words: GREATEST ACES (the high-score table's heading), THE ULTIMATE, HEAD TO HEAD, CONFLICT, CREATED BY, CASCADE GAMES, 1987, PROGRAMMED AND, BY, IAN MARTIN, GRAPHICS, DAMON REDMOND, TITLE MUSIC, ROB HUBBARD, DESIGNED BY; then the side panel's DEMO MODE, IMMORTAL, PILOT ONE and "PLANES XX".
The planes-left count's first digit in PLANES XX, written by $1D00.
The planes-left count's second digit, written by $1D05; then "  SCORE   0".
The score's five digits between two zeros (so the score shows ten times the number stored), written by $1CD4; then PILOT TWO, COMPUTER and "LEVEL ".
The computer's skill level, first digit, written by $1C9E.

The skill level's second digit, written by $1CA3; then ALL AIRCRAFT DESTROYED ($6339), and from $6C24 the four weapon names, eight characters each (" CANNON ", "HEAT  AA", "RADAR AA", "AIR-GRND"; pointers at $71F8), then the cockpit messages from $6C44, fourteen characters each, the top line and the bottom line of seven (pointers at $7432 and $7472): STALL WARNING, CRASH WARNING, PLANE CRASHED, CONTROL LOST, FUEL IS LOW, FLARE DROPPED, CHAFF DROPPED, REDUCE ALT, TO LAND, ENEMY CLOSE, NO FLARES, NO CHAFF, YOU TRAITOR, and plane one's RANGE.
Plane one's RANGE digits in message 13, written by $3BAE; then plane two's copy of the message.
Plane two's RANGE digits in message 13, written by $3BEC; then ENEMY MISSILE (message 14), FLYING OFF MAP (15) and RANGE (17).
The digits of message 17's RANGE, shared by both planes, written by $126C; then ENEMY PLANE (16) and plane one's ALT (18).
Plane one's altitude digits in message 18, written by $1298; then plane two's ALT.
Plane two's altitude digits, written by $1282; then TARGET LOCKED (19 and 20), LOCK BROKEN (21) and plane one's stock line "FLARES5" / "CHAFF 3" (22).
Plane one's flares left, the digit in FLARES5, written by $254A.
Plane one's chaff left, the digit in CHAFF 3, written by $2544; then plane two's stock line.
Plane two's flares left, written by $2559.
Plane two's chaff left, written by $2553; then MISSILE LAUNCH (23), OK FOR LANDING (24), CEILING 60000 (25), RADAR STATION (plane one's 26), ENEMY SPYSHIP (plane two's 26) and plane one's RANGE (27).
Plane one's RANGE digits in message 27, written by $3ACB; then plane two's.

Plane two's RANGE digits in message 27, written by $3B23; then OUT OF RANGE (28), a blank message (29-31), and the screen lines MISSION COMPLETED - PRESS FIRE, "    PRESS FIRE TO TAKE OFF", " COMPUTER PILOT - STANDING BY", "     TAKE OFF", "     ARM AIRCRAFT", "PAUSE  ON    " and WEAPONS ARMING SELECTION.
The two scenario descriptions' addresses, low byte then high byte: $693E (the dogfight) and $69B7 (the full-scale game), read by $640D with X = the scenario × 2.
The high bytes of the scenario description pointers, read with $6EBE (the byte after them is the first of $6EC2).

Sprite pointers for the middle of the screen, copied into sprites 0-5 of both screens by $4EA0: $A4-$A7 (the shapes at $A900-$A9FF), the top of plane two's cockpit frame, four sprites at line $9A, and $AE and $AF ($AB80 and $ABC0), the red ACE 2 logo on the side panel, expanded across.
Sprite pointers for plane two's lower cockpit frame, copied into sprites 0-3 of both screens by $4BC7: $AA-$AD, the shapes at $AA80-$AB7F.
Six sprite pointers, $36-$3B (the shapes at $8D80-$8EFF), copied into sprites 0-5 of both screens by $4651, which places the six at lines $42 and $57 of the top half, four across and two below.
Plane one's four cockpit frame sprites, pointers $3C-$3F (the shapes at $8F00-$8FFF), set by $48B7.
What pulling back (added) or pushing (taken away) adds to the turn rate, by the bank: nothing up to bank 3, then 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 26, 50, 50.
The low bytes of the four tracer frames' masks in page $9D ($9D48, $9D68, $9D88, $9DA8), patched into the AND at $1893 by the frame $74.
The screen offsets of the four tracer cells from the first ($1884, $18B0): 0, 39, 78 and 117, each one row down and one column left of the last.
The pitch's cosine as a fraction of 256, by the pitch ($77, 0-23): $FF level, then down by 8 a step to $C0, by 16 to 0 at pitch 20. $429B multiplies the speed by it for the ground speed.
The cockpit view's scale for an elevation ($3965): 64 entries for 0-63, rising slowly then faster (0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 ... $2D, $30, $33, $36 ... ).

How often the stick changes the pitch, by the bank ($2A04): added into $72 each pass, and the stick acts on a carry; $FF level, falling to $A3 by bank 7 and to 0 at bank 15, where the stick no longer moves the nose.

The cockpit messages' letters ($17F3): for each character code, the place of its five-byte picture in the small font at $9500. Codes 0-9 (digit values) and $30-$39 give 0, 5, 10 ... 45; space ($20) $3C, - $32, . $37; the enciphered letters $41-$5A give the real letters' places, A at $41 to Y at $B9, five apart. The table runs to $6FC0 and so shares its bytes with the cipher at $6F7F.

The text cipher, read as $6F7F + the stored letter ($1911, $35F1, $56DA): for $41-$59, the real letter, in the bytes $6FC0-$6FD8 (A means H, B R, C F, D L, E K, F T, G J, H N, I U, J Y, K E, L X, M O, N W, O G, P C, Q D, R B, S A, T S, U M, V P, W I, X V, Y Q); $5A, where Z would be, gives a 0 byte ($6FD9), so no stored code gives Z. The bytes before $6FC0 are the message glyph table above.
For each roll quarter, 0 or 1, EORed with the pitch direction ($7C) into $F3, which chooses ADD or SUBTRACT for the horizon's crossing column ($318A).
For each roll quarter, 0 or 1, EORed with the pitch direction into $F4, which chooses ADD or SUBTRACT for the horizon's row ($31B2).
The horizon's first slope value by the bank (0-15), into $C1: 0, $1F, $24 ... rising to $FF; like a sine of the bank.
The second slope value by the bank, into $C2: 16 entries, $6FF1-$7000, $FF falling to 0; like its cosine.
The keyboard row masks for $DC00 in the order the controls read them ($369A): rows 7, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 0 ($7F, $FD, $FB, $F7, $EF, $DF, $BF, $FE).
A missile hit's damage by the MISSILE HITS TO KILL option ($263F): 255 for one hit, 128 for two, 96 for three (entry 0 is not used).
The screen offset of each of the 25 rows, row × 40, low bytes; added to a screen's base by every routine that prints or draws on the screen.
The high bytes of row × 40, for the same 25 rows.
The screen offset of column 10 of each of the 25 rows (row × 40 + 10), low bytes, for the cockpit halves ($216E, $2210).
The high bytes of row × 40 + 10.

The horizon's edge-character list for each bank ($320F, X = the bank × 2), low byte then high byte: $709E for banks 0 and 1, then $70A6, $70AD, $70B3, $70B8, $70BC, $70BF, $70C1, $70C2, $70C4, $70C7, $70CB, $70D0 and $70D6 for banks 2-14 (bank 15 would read the first bytes of $708F).
The high bytes of the edge-list pointers, read with $7071.

The length of each bank's edge-character list ($3221, by the bank): 1, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 11 for banks 0-14; then from $709E the lists themselves, character codes $DC (sky) and $DE-$E4 (the edge shapes copied in by $338E).
For each bank, how many columns the horizon line moves at each step ($3246): 30 for level, 8, 7 ... down to 1 from bank 8.
For each bank, how many rows each step covers ($324B): 1 up to bank 8, then 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 11 and 8.
The fill shapes for a view with no horizon ($3433) and the horizon's fill characters: eight bytes of $55 (sky, colour 1 in every pixel) and eight of $FF (ground, colour 3).
The high bytes of the edge shape pointers, read with $7111.
For each bank, the number of edge shape bytes to copy less one ($339A): 1 for banks 0 and 15, $37 (seven characters) for banks 1 and 2, down to 7 at bank 8 and up to $2F again.
The partial cell of an instrument bar ($3455, $349D): one, two, three or four double pixels filled from the left ($C0, $F0, $FC, $FF).

Plane one's bank indicator: the low byte, in page $97, of the index table for each quarter of the roll ($9740, $97C0, $9780, $9700), patched into $19D3; each says where in the panel graphics at $A1F0 the picture's 63 bytes go.
The colour RAM places (low bytes, three rows of four) of plane one's instrument faces, coloured brown by $46FB.
The pitch ladder's mark row by the pitch ($1A70, $1B61), 24 entries: row 9 for level, moving out to row 19.
The mark row by the pitch for the other direction ($1A67, $1B58): row 9 for level, moving out to row 0 by pitch 14 and staying there.
Plane one's compass pictures, seven pointers low byte then high byte ($99C8, $99F8, $9A20, $9A50, $9A81, $9AB4, $9AE8), picked by $1ABF through $71A5.
The high bytes of plane one's compass picture pointers.
Plane two's compass pictures, seven pointers ($EEA2, $EECF, $EEFF, $EF37, $EF6F, $EFA9, $EFE4), picked by $1B90.
The high bytes of plane two's compass picture pointers.
The heading in sixteenths to the compass picture (0-6): 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, then back down 6 to 0 for the other half of the circle, which is drawn mirrored.
Plane one's compass: the low byte, in page $97, of the index table for each quarter of the heading ($9700, $9780, $97C0, $9740).
Plane two's compass: the low bytes of the byte-order list for each quarter ($7259, $72A1, $7301, $7389).
The high bytes of plane two's compass byte-order lists, read with $71B9.
The picture's width and height in cells by its size $5E (0-2): 1, 2 or 3 ($16AF).
For each roll quarter, 0 or $FF: a sign used by $3948 when it turns a point by the roll.
A second sign for each roll quarter, 0 or $FF, for $3948.
A third sign for each roll quarter, 0 or $FF, for $3948.
The map picture's twelve rows, 30 characters each from $9800: low bytes of $9800 + 30 × the row ($14DB).
The high bytes of the map row pointers.
The missile sight's box, four pictures of 72 bytes ($9C28, $9C70, $9CB8, $9D00), low byte then high byte, picked by the signs of the enemy's fine position ($05, $06; $23C5-$23D5).
The high bytes of the box picture pointers.
Four more pointers in the same form ($9D48, $9D90, $9DD8, $9E20) that the index at $23D5 never reaches; those addresses hold other tables.
The four weapon names' addresses for the weapon panel ($5F91): $6C24 CANNON, $6C2C HEAT AA, $6C34 RADAR AA, $6C3C AIR-GRND; low byte then high byte.
The high bytes of the weapon name pointers; the next 65 bytes, $7200-$7240, hold a falling curve from $FF to 0 (a quarter of a cosine) that nothing in the code addresses and no run of the game read.

The byte orders for a picture's four frames, by size ($1581: 8 bytes a size, 2 a frame): one cell $7259, $7259, $7341, $7341; two cells $7259, $7369, $7349, $7329; three cells $7259, $7389, $72A1, $7301. Frames 1 and 3 are also mirrored through $9000, so the four frames are the picture as drawn, mirrored left to right, upside down, and turned half round.

The high bytes of the byte-order pointers. From $7259, the lists themselves, each an offset into the picture for every byte built: $7259 in order (0 to 71); $72A1 each column of 24 bytes upside down; $7301 all 72 reversed, whose tail is also the 32-byte list at $7329 and the 8-byte list at $7341; $7349 each 16-byte column upside down; $7369 the two 16-byte columns swapped; $7389 the three columns of 24 in reverse order. Plane two's bank indicator and compass use the 72-byte lists by the quarter of the roll or heading. The 24 bytes $72E9-$7300 (a fourth upside-down column) are past every list's end.

The side panel's screen codes, read as $73B1 + the character ($1915): from $73E1, the digits 0-9 to codes 0-9, A to $0B, C $0C, D $0D, E $0E, W $0F, I $10, L $11, M $12, N $13, O to 0 (the zero), P $14, R $15, S $16, T $17, U $18, V $19, and every other character to $0A, a blank. Its first 32 bytes are the end of the byte-order list at $7389.
The climb rate by the pitch, as a fraction of the speed ($4302): 0, $2A, $4D ... $C8, then $D2 from pitch 18 on.
The powers of ten for $3ED4, low bytes: 10000, 1000, 100, 10, 1.
Their high bytes ($27, $03, 0, 0, 0).

Pilot one's 32 cockpit messages, pointers low byte then high byte into the texts at $6C44 ($2EE8): 0 STALL WARNING, 1 CRASH WARNING, 2 PLANE CRASHED, 3 CONTROL LOST, 4 FUEL IS LOW, 5 FLARE DROPPED, 6 CHAFF DROPPED, 7 REDUCE ALT, 8 TO LAND, 9 ENEMY CLOSE, 10 NO FLARES, 11 NO CHAFF, 12 YOU TRAITOR, 13 RANGE, 14 ENEMY MISSILE, 15 FLYING OFF MAP, 16 ENEMY PLANE, 17 RANGE, 18 ALT, 19 and 20 TARGET LOCKED, 21 LOCK BROKEN, 22 the flares and chaff left, 23 MISSILE LAUNCH, 24 OK FOR LANDING, 25 CEILING 60000, 26 RADAR STATION, 27 RANGE, 28 OUT OF RANGE, 29-31 blank.
The high bytes of pilot one's message pointers.
Pilot two's 32 cockpit messages, the same list but with its own copies of the messages that carry figures (13, 18, 22, 27) and ENEMY SPYSHIP for 26 ($2F6A).
The high bytes of pilot two's message pointers.

The video chip's registers $D000-$D02E for the title, copied by $0AAC: eight sprites in a row at the foot of the screen (sprites 0-3 and 4-7 both at across $88, $A0, $B8, $D0, down $DC), all on, 4-7 multicoloured, the multicolours light grey and blue, sprites 0-3 dark grey and 4-7 medium grey: the CASCADE logo.

The title sprites' pointers ($0AB7): $DA-$DD (the shapes at $B680, from $D100) and $9A-$9D ($A680, from $D000). Then, from $74E9, plane one's dogfight loadout, eight bytes: 3000 cannon rounds ($0BB8), 8 heat seekers, no radar missiles, none of the third kind.

Plane one's full-scale loadout, eight bytes: the cannon rounds (3000), then the heat seekers, radar missiles and the third kind as words. The demo swaps eight bytes in here ($0BF6) and puts them back ($598D).
Plane one's heat seekers in the full-scale game (6), set by the arming screen ($5905).
Plane one's radar missiles (4), set by the arming screen ($590A).

Plane one's air-to-ground missiles (0), set by the arming screen ($590F); then plane two's dogfight loadout from $74F9 (3000 rounds, 8 heat seekers) and the start of its full-scale one at $7501 (3000 rounds).
Plane two's heat seekers in the full-scale game (6), set by the arming screen or by the computer's choice ($1177).
Plane two's radar missiles (4).
Plane two's air-to-ship missiles (0).
The computer's air-to-air choice for plane two ($1174): 8 heat seekers, 4 radar missiles, none of the third kind.
The computer's other choice ($1187): 4 heat seekers, no radar missiles, 2 air-to-ship missiles.
The ACE 2 logo's top row, 13 character codes ($C0 up, five apart; $FF a blank cell between ACE and 2), drawn by $38E8.
The logo's second row of character codes ($C1 up).
The logo's third row ($C2 up).
The logo's fourth row ($C3 up).
The logo's bottom row ($C4 up). The eight bytes after it, $7556-$755D, read "S0:QZ", $FF, "QZ" in plain ASCII, a disk command (scratch the file QZ) that nothing uses.
The five high-score entries' names in the table at $0903-$09FF, pointers low byte then high byte: $0934, $0941, $094E, $095B, $0968 (13 bytes apart).
The high bytes of the high-score name pointers.
Plane one's loadout by the scenario, low byte then high byte: $74E9 (dogfight) and $74F1 (full-scale), for $2F97.
The high bytes of plane one's loadout pointers.
Plane two's loadouts: $74F9 (dogfight) and $7501 (full-scale).
The high bytes of plane two's loadout pointers.

A ground target's close picture by our roll (0-63, $0272; $6138 and $617F): the low four bits pick one of eight pictures (the pointers at $7820-$7851), the high four bits the frame, 0 or, for the upside-down half of the roll, 3 (the picture turned half round); the last four entries are 0.

The enemy's large picture, last step of $2C86 ($2DD4): 88 entries, by the previous step's result (low four bits × 8) and our pitch added to its high four bits (modulo 8), each a picture code: the low four bits pick one of the pictures at $77F8, the high four bits the frame.
The third step of the large picture's lookup ($2DBA): 64 entries, each a result whose high four bits get our pitch class added and whose low four bits pick a row of $75B0.
The second step ($2D9D): 48 entries picked by the first step's low four bits × 8 and its high four bits plus our roll in eighths (modulo 8); each picks an entry of $7608.

The large picture's lookup ($2C86): from $76B8, 320 bytes, five blocks of 64 by the enemy's pitch (level, climbing, steep climb, diving, steep dive; the block offsets at $7816), each indexed by its roll in eighths and its direction relative to ours in eighths, which give an entry of the first 64 bytes, $7678-$76B7 ($2D83); those pick an entry of $7648.
The enemy's large pictures, fifteen pointers low byte then high byte, 32 bytes apart from $FE00 to $FFC0 ($2DE5), each the picture's bytes that $1581 builds it from.
The high bytes of the large picture pointers.
The offsets of the five pitch blocks in the large picture's first table ($2D53): 0, $40, $80, $C0 and $100, words, low byte first.
The high bytes of the pitch block offsets, read with $7816.
The spy ship's one-cell pictures (the target over the sea, $38 = 0): eight pointers low byte then high byte, $9B88 to $9BC0, eight bytes apart ($6157).
The high bytes of the spy ship's one-cell picture pointers.
The spy ship's two-cell pictures: eight pointers, $FAA0 to $FB80, 32 bytes apart ($6192).
The high bytes of the spy ship's two-cell picture pointers.
The radar station's one-cell pictures (the target over land, $38 = 1): eight pointers, $FBA0 to $FBD8, eight bytes apart ($614B).
The high bytes of the radar station's one-cell picture pointers.
The radar station's two-cell pictures: eight pointers, $FBE0 to $FCC0, 32 bytes apart ($619E).
The high bytes of the radar station's two-cell picture pointers.

A missile's top speed by its type ($2684): 250 for the heat seeker (type 1), 255 for the radar missile (2); the entries for type 0 (0) and type 3 ($D2) are not read, since the air-to-ground missile flies by $27D4. After them, from $7864, bytes the program never reads, left in memory when the disk was made: "C1CX", the disk commands "S0:C1" and "S0:CX" (scratch the files C1 and CX), twelve bytes $7874-$787F, and then, from $7880 to $7FFD, a byte-for-byte copy of $3000-$377D.
Never run or read: the first 1024 bytes of a copy of $3000-$377D, byte for byte the code at $3000-$33FF, left in memory when the disk was made.
The rest of the unused copy: the same bytes as $3400-$377D.
The loader's start address, $0900: it jumps through here when every track is in ($CB6B).

Plane two's instrument panel character set, as the hand-over leaves it: the video chip shows it for the bottom panel, rows 20-24. While the title runs, the title's big font is here instead, because $53D4 swaps this 2 KB with $D800-$DFFF at each start of the title and of a game. The rest of the sector repeats the high-score sector from its 18th byte, because SAVE OPTIONS lays the 17 bytes over the buffer at $CF00 and writes all 256 ($1EA5).

Rob Hubbard's music driver, called once a tick of the music clock from the title interrupt ($43DE) and, while the music is on, from the play interrupt ($4447). Volume 15 with the low-pass filter ($D418 = $1F) every call. The mode byte $E574 decides what it does: $40 restarts the tune (each voice's track and pattern positions, note length, waveform and release cleared, instrument 10, the silent one, selected), after which the byte is left at $0A and the tune plays; 0 to $3F plays; $C0 silences all three voices and leaves $80; $80 does nothing. Three voices (X from $E623 = 2 down to 0, SID register offsets 0, 7 and 14 at $E54C).

The tempo: $E572 counts 3 to 0 and $E570 counts down from the tempo $E571 (1). A voice reads its next note step only when $E572 is not 0 and $E570 equals $E571, which happens on three calls in every eight, spaced 3, 2 and 3 calls apart; on the other calls only the running effects are updated.

For each voice: on a note step, count down the note's length ($E556); while it lasts, only check whether its release is due ($E1D7). When it runs out, read the next note: the voice's track list (pointers at $E67C/$E67F: $E6CE, $E712 and $E7CB) gives the pattern number at the track position $E550.
A track byte of $80 or more ends the list: the track, the pattern position and the length start again from 0, so the tune loops.

Point $FE/$FF at the pattern (38 patterns, pointers at $E682/$E6A8), clear the slide, the frames since the note ($E587) and the drum-table position, set the filter sweep's start ($30), open the gate mask ($E953 = $FF), and read the note's first byte: bits 0-4 its length in steps less one, bit 5 hold the gate to the end, bit 6 a rest, bit 7 another byte follows. That byte, when it is $80 or more, starts a slide ($EB48) and the byte after it is the slide's speed ($E578); below $80 it selects the instrument ($EA46).

The note byte: bits 0-6 the note (0 to 95, kept in $E90F), whose frequency comes from the table at $E48A; bit 7 set leaves the instrument's envelope and pulse width running from the note before, which slurs one note into the next.
A rest: gate off, attack, decay, sustain and release all 0, and the waveform byte 8 (the test bit), which silences the voice at once.

Start the instrument (8 bytes from $E5CB and 8 from $E624, both at the instrument number × 8): unless the note slurs, the pulse width, attack/decay and sustain/release go straight to the chip, the pulse sweep's direction is reset and the instrument's frame count ($E627) is loaded into $E584. Its waveform ($E5CD) becomes the voice's waveform. Then step past the note; a pattern ending in $FF moves the voice on to the next pattern of its track.
Still inside a note: on its last step, unless bit 5 held it, close the gate ($E953 = $FE) so the release begins.

The effects, every call. Vibrato when the instrument's byte 5 is not 0: bits 3-6 its depth, bits 0-2 a shift. The offset $E000 runs up and down between 0 and the depth, one a call; once the note's first four frames have passed (and unless a slide is running) the frequency is the note's, less half the depth in steps, plus the offset in steps, where a step is the gap from the note below shifted right by the shift.

The pulse-width sweep when the instrument's byte 6 is not 0: that speed is added to the 12-bit pulse width until its top four bits reach the limit in the high half of the second table's byte 5, then taken away until they reach the limit in its low half; the two halves are written into the comparisons at $E2DD and $E2F7.
The upper limit of the pulse sweep, written by $E2C4 from the high half of the instrument's second-table byte 5 ($0F, or $0C for instrument 3).
The lower limit of the pulse sweep, written by $E2BA from the low half of the same byte (0 for instruments 0, 3 and 5; 8, 7 and $0D for instruments 7, 8 and 9).

The slide: a slide byte from $80 to $BE raises the frequency each call by its low six bits × 256 plus the speed $E578; from $BF to $FF it lowers it the same way. The high part goes into the operands at $E32A and $E344.
The high byte of the downward slide's step, written by $E319.

The high byte of the upward slide's step, written by $E333. Then the drum table, when the instrument's effect byte has bit 7 and the note is no rest: from the pointer in the second table's bytes 0-1 and the voice's position $EBC7, an entry of a byte of $80 or more (but $85) and a frequency high byte goes straight to the chip; a byte below $80 is the waveform, and the two bytes after it are taken from the frequency; $85 holds the last sound. Instruments 1, 2, 4 and 6 are drums.

Effect bit 1: the waveform alternates each frame between the instrument's and the second table's byte 2 (no instrument here sets it). Effect bit 2: for the instrument's frame count, the second table's byte 1 is the waveform (instrument 3 starts with a frame of noise, instruments 7, 8 and 9 with a few of synchronised pulse), then the instrument's own; it skips the arpeggio.

Effect bit 5, the filter sweep: the cutoff ($E58D, from $30 at each note) moves by the second table's byte 7 a call and goes to $D416, with byte 6 into $D417 (resonance, and the voices filtered). Only instrument 0 sets it: down 3 a call, resonance 15, voice 3 filtered.

Effect bit 6: while the frame count runs, the voice plays the note in the second table's byte 0 instead of its own (instrument 3, the only one with the bit, note $42), then the note's own frequency again.
